Tight Lower Bounds for Stochastic Nonconvex-Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization

Siqi Zhang ††thanks: School of Management and Engineering, Nanjing University, siqi.zhang@nju.edu.cn    Qilong Wu ††thanks: School of Data Science, the Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen), qilongwu@link.cuhk.edu.cn    Junchi Yang ††thanks: School of Data Science, the Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen), yangjunchi@cuhk.edu.cn
September 28, 2026
Abstract

We study the stochastic first-order oracle complexity of finding ϵ\epsilon-stationary points of the primal function in smooth nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization. For sufficiently small ϵ\epsilon, we establish lower bounds of Ω⁡(κ​L​Δ​σ2​ϵ−4)\Omega(\kappa L\Delta\sigma^{2}\epsilon^{-4}) under the bounded-variance assumption and Ω⁡(κ3/2​L¯​Δ​σ​ϵ−3)\Omega(\kappa^{3/2}\bar{L}\Delta\sigma\epsilon^{-3}) under the additional assumption of averaged smoothness. Here, LL and L¯\bar{L} denote the smoothness and averaged-smoothness constants, respectively, Δ\Delta is the initial primal gap, σ2\sigma^{2} bounds the oracle variance, and κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu or L¯/μ\bar{L}/\mu in the respective settings, where μ\mu is the strong-concavity parameter. Our bounded-variance lower bound improves the dependence on the condition number from κ1/3\kappa^{1/3} in previous lower bounds to κ\kappa, while our averaged-smoothness lower bound is the first of its kind. In both settings, the resulting lower bounds match existing upper bounds in their dependence on κ\kappa and ϵ\epsilon. Our proofs are based on a unified quadratic lifting construction that transfers a hardness instance for stochastic nonconvex minimization to unconstrained minimax optimization while preserving the required variance and smoothness properties.

1 Introduction

We consider the nonconvex-strongly-concave (NC-SC) minimax problem

minx∈ℝdx⁡Φ⁡(x),Φ⁡(x):=maxy∈ℝdy⁡f⁡(x,y),\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}}\Phi(x),\qquad\Phi(x):=\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}}f(x,y), (1)

where ff has an LL-Lipschitz gradient and f⁡(x,⋅)f(x,\cdot) is μ\mu-strongly concave. Problems of this form arise in a variety of machine learning applications (Sinha et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019; Zhu et al., 2023). Strong concavity ensures that the inner maximizer is unique, and the resulting primal function Φ\Phi is differentiable, although generally nonconvex. A central goal is to find a point x^\hat{x} such that ‖∇Φ​(x^)‖≤ϵ\left\lVert\nabla\Phi(\hat{x})\right\rVert\leq{\epsilon}, using stochastic gradients of ff. In the deterministic and finite-sum settings, accelerated proximal-point methods achieve the optimal complexity 𝒪⁡(κ​ϵ−2)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}\epsilon^{-2}), where κ≜L/μ\kappa\triangleq L/\mu is the condition number, already matching the corresponding lower bounds (Lin et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2021; Han et al., 2024).

In the stochastic setting, where f⁡(x,y)≜𝔼ξ​[F⁡(x,y,ξ)]f(x,y)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[F(x,y;\xi)], two common oracle assumptions lead to different complexity guarantees. Under an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle with uniformly bounded variance, existing algorithms achieve complexity 𝒪⁡(κ​ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}(\kappa{\epsilon}^{-4}) (Zhang et al., 2024). With the additional assumption of averaged smoothness of the stochastic gradients, the best known upper bounds improve to 𝒪⁡(ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}({\epsilon}^{-3}) (Luo et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026). However, the corresponding lower bounds remain incomplete. Under bounded variance, Li et al. (2021) established an Ω⁡(κ1/3​ϵ−4)\Omega(\kappa^{1/3}{\epsilon}^{-4}) lower bound for constrained NC-SC problems, leaving a gap in the dependence on κ\kappa relative to the 𝒪⁡(κ​ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}(\kappa{\epsilon}^{-4}) upper bound. Under averaged smoothness, to the best of our knowledge, no lower bound has been established specifically for NC-SC minimax optimization. We therefore ask:

Can we establish tight lower bounds for stochastic NC-SC minimax optimization under bounded variance and averaged smoothness?

Contributions

In this work, we answer both questions affirmatively. Our contributions are three-fold. First, let ϵ>0\epsilon>0 denote the target accuracy and assume Φ⁡(0)−infxΦ⁡(x)≤Δ\Phi(0)-\inf_{x}\Phi(x)\leq\Delta. For an unbiased bounded-variance (BV) oracle11 1 Concurrent work by Zhou (2026) independently establishes an Ω⁡(κ​ϵ−4)\Omega(\kappa\epsilon^{-4}) lower bound for the BV setting. Our work differs in considering fully unconstrained settings, and additionally establishes lower bounds under averaged smoothness. with variance bounded by σ2\sigma^{2}, we establish the lower bound, with κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu,

Ω⁡(κ​L​σ2​Δϵ4).\Omega\!\left(\frac{\kappa L\sigma^{2}\Delta}{{\epsilon}^{4}}\right). (2)

Second, for an averaged-smooth (AS) oracle with Lipschitz constant L¯\bar{L}, we establish, with κ=L¯/μ\kappa=\bar{L}/\mu,

Ω⁡(L¯​Δϵ2​min⁡{κ​σ2ϵ2,κ3/2​σϵ}).\Omega\!\left(\frac{\overline{L}\Delta}{{\epsilon}^{2}}\min\left\{\frac{\kappa\sigma^{2}}{{\epsilon}^{2}},\frac{\kappa^{3/2}\sigma}{{\epsilon}}\right\}\right). (3)

We refer to Theorems 4.1 and 5.1 for the formal statements, and summarize the comparison with existing results in Table 1 and Figure 1. In the BV setting, our lower bound (2) improves the dependence on κ\kappa over the previous lower bound of Li et al. (2021) and matches the upper complexity bounds of Zhang et al. (2024) and Zhang et al. (2026) in their dependence on both κ\kappa and ϵ\epsilon. To the best of our knowledge, (3) is the first lower bound specifically for the AS setting. Moreover, this lower bound matches the upper complexity bound of Zhang et al. (2026) in its dependence on κ\kappa and ϵ\epsilon when ϵ−1≳κ\epsilon^{-1}\gtrsim\sqrt{\kappa}, and that of Zhang et al. (2022b) when ϵ−1≲κ\epsilon^{-1}\lesssim\sqrt{\kappa}.

Finally, we note that the corresponding upper bounds are stated under slightly different problem classes and measures of initial optimality. Specifically, Zhang et al. (2024) and Zhang et al. (2026) use a Moreau-envelope-based stationarity measurement. To facilitate a more direct comparison, we also establish lower bounds using a Moreau envelope stationarity, see Corollary 5.2.

The hard instance is obtained through a quadratic lifting of hard instances for stochastic nonconvex minimization (Carmon et al., 2020; Arjevani et al., 2023). Starting from the hard instance FTF_{T} by Carmon et al. (2020), we construct a minimax objective of the form

fT​(x,y)=α​FT​(β​y)−ν2​‖y−γ​x‖2,f_{T}(x,y)=\alpha F_{T}(\beta y)-\frac{\nu}{2}\|y-\gamma x\|^{2},

where the parameters α,β,ν\alpha,\beta,\nu and γ\gamma are chosen so that fT​(x,⋅)f_{T}(x,\cdot) is strongly-concave. The quadratic coupling is designed so that stationarity of the primal function ΦT​(x)=maxy⁡fT​(x,y)\Phi_{T}(x)=\max_{y}f_{T}(x,y) implies approximate stationarity of FTF_{T} at the explicitly rescaled point β​γ​x\beta\gamma x. In particular, an ϵ{\epsilon}-stationary point x^\hat{x} of ΦT\Phi_{T} yields an appropriately scaled approximate stationary point β​γ​x^\beta\gamma\hat{x} of FTF_{T}. Since this point is obtained directly from x^\hat{x}, the reduction does not require computing the inner maximizer and therefore introduces no additional oracle cost. The construction is compatible with stochastic oracle: we keep the quadratic coupling deterministic and introduce randomness only through the stochastic oracle associated with FTF_{T}, preventing the oracle variance from growing with ‖x‖\|x\| or ‖y‖\|y\| over the unconstrained domain. The main technical challenge is therefore to establish this stationarity-preserving reduction and tune the scaling parameters so that the lifted instance simultaneously satisfies the required smoothness, strong-concavity and variance conditions.

2 Related Literature

Lower Bounds for Minimax Optimization.

First-order oracle lower bounds for convex-concave and strongly-convex-strongly-concave minimax problems were established by Ouyang and Xu (2021) and Zhang et al. (2022a), while Xie et al. (2020) studied the finite-sum setting. For nonconvex-strongly-concave (NC-SC) problems, Zhang et al. (2021) derived lower bounds for both the deterministic and averaged-smooth finite-sum settings. Han et al. (2024) further studied finite-sum NC-SC problems under an oracle model that allows access to both component gradients and proximal operators. Closest to our setting, Li et al. (2021) established deterministic and stochastic lower bounds for NC-SC problems; under bounded variance, their stochastic lower bound contains the term Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ1/3​σ2​ϵ−4)\Omega(L\Delta\kappa^{1/3}\sigma^{2}{\epsilon}^{-4}). For a broader overview of oracle-complexity results in minimization and minimax optimization, we refer to Zhang and Hu (2025).

Nonconvex Minimax Optimization Algorithms.

In the deterministic NC-SC setting, accelerated proximal-point methods achieve near-optimal dependence on the condition number (Lin et al., 2020a; Zhang et al., 2021). In the stochastic setting, two-timescale SGDA attains 𝒪⁡(κ3​ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{3}{\epsilon}^{-4}) stochastic gradient complexity under bounded variance (Lin et al., 2020b; Lin et al., 2025), while SREDA achieves 𝒪⁡(κ3​ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{3}{\epsilon}^{-3}) under averaged smoothness (Luo et al., 2020). Momentum-based and adaptive variants have also been developed (Huang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023). SAPD+ combines a proximal-point framework with accelerated saddle-point solvers and also admits a variance-reduced variant (Zhang et al., 2024). More recently, Zhang et al. (2026) proposed the single-loop methods SPDE and VR-SPDE, with complexities 𝒪⁡(κ​ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}(\kappa{\epsilon}^{-4}) under bounded variance and 𝒪⁡(κ3/2​ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{3/2}{\epsilon}^{-3}) under averaged smoothness, respectively. These rates match the (κ,ϵ)(\kappa,{\epsilon}) dependence of the stochastic terms in our lower bounds. Table 1 summarizes the rates of these methods. Beyond the NC-SC setting, Li et al. (2026) study smoothing and dual perturbation for nonconvex-concave problems, while Zhang and Xu (2026) develop single-loop methods that attain rates previously achieved by multi-loop schemes. Recent work on NC-SC problems considers generalized smoothness (Gao and Liu, 2026) and regularized Newton methods (Ma et al., 2026).

Recent Lower Bounds beyond Strong Concavity.

Recent work has extended lower-bound analyses to minimax problems in which strong concavity is relaxed to concavity or the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition. For NC-C problems with a compact dual domain, Wu et al. (2026) establish deterministic and stochastic lower bounds of Ω⁡(ϵ−3)\Omega({\epsilon}^{-3}) and Ω⁡(ϵ−6)\Omega({\epsilon}^{-6}), respectively, for zero-respecting algorithms under Moreau-envelope stationarity. Deterministic lower bounds for projected zero-respecting methods are also developed by Zhang and Xu (2026). Pan et al. (2026) establish the Ω⁡(ϵ−3)\Omega({\epsilon}^{-3}) deterministic lower bound for arbitrary first-order algorithms and provide a matching upper bound. For NC-PL problems, Pan and Li (2026) establish an Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ​ϵ−2)\Omega(L\Delta\kappa{\epsilon}^{-2}) lower bound for arbitrary deterministic first-order methods, matching the known upper bound in the corresponding parameter regime. In particular, their result demonstrates that relaxing strong concavity to the PL condition can lead to a stronger dependence on the condition number κ\kappa in the deterministic setting. In contrast, our work focuses on stochastic NC-SC problems and characterizes how the bounded-variance and averaged-smoothness oracle models determine the dependence on κ\kappa.

3 Problem Setup and Oracle Complexity

We use Euclidean norms, denote z=(x,y)z=(x,y), and supp⁡(z)≜{i:zi≠0}\operatorname{supp}(z)\triangleq\{i:z_{i}\neq 0\} denote the support of z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. For a mapping TT between Euclidean spaces, we denote

Lip(T)≜inf{C≥0:∥T(u)−T(v)∥≤C∥u−v∥,∀u,v}\operatorname{Lip}(T)\triangleq\inf\left\{C\geq 0:\|T(u)-T(v)\|\leq C\|u-v\|,\ \forall\,u,v\right\}

as its global Lipschitz constant. Here we study the lower bound under the oracle complexity framework (Nemirovskij and Yudin, 1983), which comes with the following components: a function class, a stochastic oracle, an algorithm class, and a convergence criterion. We will discuss them in details in this section.

Function class.

We consider nonconvex-strongly-concave (NC-SC) objectives. For M,μ,Δ>0M,\mu,\Delta>0, let ℱdx,dy​(M,μ,Δ)\mathcal{F}^{d_{x},d_{y}}(M,\mu,\Delta) denote the set of continuously differentiable functions f:ℝdx×ℝdy→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}\to\mathbb{R} such that, with z=(x,y)z=(x,y), Φ⁡(x)≜maxy⁡f⁡(x,y)\Phi(x)\triangleq\max_{y}f(x,y), Φ∗≜infxΦ⁡(x)>−∞\Phi_{*}\triangleq\inf_{x}\Phi(x)>-\infty,

‖∇f​(z)−∇f​(z′)‖≤M⁡‖z−z′‖\displaystyle\left\lVert\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(z^{\prime})\right\rVert\leq M\left\lVert z-z^{\prime}\right\rVert ∀z,z′∈ℝdx+dy,\displaystyle\forall z,z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}+d_{y}}, (4)
f⁡(x,y′)≤f⁡(x,y)+⟨∇yf​(x,y),y′−y⟩−μ2​‖y′−y‖2\displaystyle f(x,y^{\prime})\leq f(x,y)+\left\langle\nabla_{y}f(x,y),y^{\prime}-y\right\rangle-\frac{\mu}{2}\left\lVert y^{\prime}-y\right\rVert^{2} ∀x∈ℝdx,y,y′∈ℝdy,\displaystyle\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}},\;y,y^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}, (5)
Φ⁡(0)−Φ∗≤Δ.\displaystyle\Phi(0)-\Phi_{*}\leq\Delta. (6)

Both the primal and dual variables are unconstrained, and no convexity in xx is imposed. Strong concavity ensures that the inner maximizer y∗​(x)y^{*}(x) exists and is unique for every xx. Moreover, Φ\Phi is differentiable with ∇Φ​(x)=∇xf​(x,y∗​(x))\nabla\Phi(x)=\nabla_{x}f(x,y^{*}(x)), is MM-weakly convex, and has an M⁡(1+M/μ)M(1+M/\mu)-Lipschitz gradient. These properties hold without any compactness assumption; see Appendix A.

Oracle class.

We consider stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) (Arjevani et al., 2023). An instance is a pair (f,G)(f,G), including the law of the random seed ξ\xi. The oracle is a measurable random vector field and returns a joint gradient estimate G⁡(z,ξ)=(Gx​(z,ξ),Gy​(z,ξ))G(z;\xi)=(G_{x}(z;\xi),G_{y}(z;\xi)) such that, for every zz,

𝔼ξ​G​(z,ξ)=∇f​(z),𝔼ξ​‖G⁡(z,ξ)−∇f​(z)‖2≤σ2.\mathbb{E}_{\xi}G(z;\xi)=\nabla f(z),\qquad\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left\lVert G(z;\xi)-\nabla f(z)\right\rVert^{2}\leq\sigma^{2}. (7)

The bounded-variance (BV) class ℐBV​(L,μ,Δ,σ)\mathcal{I}_{\rm BV}(L,\mu,\Delta,\sigma) requires f∈ℱdx,dy​(L,μ,Δ)f\in\mathcal{F}^{d_{x},d_{y}}(L,\mu,\Delta) and Equation (7). The averaged-smooth (AS) class ℐAS​(L¯,μ,Δ,σ)\mathcal{I}_{\rm AS}(\overline{L},\mu,\Delta,\sigma) requires f∈ℱdx,dy​(L¯,μ,Δ)f\in\mathcal{F}^{d_{x},d_{y}}(\overline{L},\mu,\Delta), Equation (7), and

𝔼ξ​‖G⁡(z,ξ)−G⁡(z′,ξ)‖2≤L¯2​‖z−z′‖2for all ​z,z′.\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left\lVert G(z;\xi)-G(z^{\prime};\xi)\right\rVert^{2}\leq\overline{L}^{2}\left\lVert z-z^{\prime}\right\rVert^{2}\qquad\text{for all }z,z^{\prime}. (8)

Here, the same random seed ξ\xi is used to evaluate GG at zz and z′z^{\prime}. By unbiasedness and Jensen’s inequality, ‖∇f​(z)−∇f​(z′)‖2≤𝔼ξ​‖G⁡(z,ξ)−G⁡(z′,ξ)‖2\left\lVert\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(z^{\prime})\right\rVert^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left\lVert G(z;\xi)-G(z^{\prime};\xi)\right\rVert^{2}, so Equation (8) implies that ∇f\nabla f is L¯\overline{L}-Lipschitz. Accordingly, we define the condition number as κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu in the BV setting and κ=L¯/μ\kappa=\overline{L}/\mu in the AS setting.

3.1 Algorithm Class and Lower Bound

Oracle access.

At round tt, an algorithm selects 1≤Kt≤K1\leq K_{t}\leq K points zt,1,…,zt,Ktz^{t,1},\ldots,z^{t,K_{t}} using its past responses and internal randomness. A fresh independent seed ξt\xi_{t} is then drawn, and the oracle returns G⁡(zt,1,ξt),…,G⁡(zt,Kt,ξt)G(z^{t,1};\xi_{t}),\ldots,G(z^{t,K_{t}};\xi_{t}). The current points are chosen before any current response is observed; the seed is hidden and cannot be queried again later. We take K=1K=1 in BV and any fixed finite KK in AS; K=2K=2 permits paired same-sample differences.

Algorithm class.

We consider zero-respecting stochastic first-order algorithms. Let gt,k=G⁡(zt,k,ξt)g^{t,k}=G(z^{t,k};\xi_{t}) and define the coordinates revealed before round tt by

𝒮t=⋃s<t⋃j=1Kssupp⁡(gs,j).\mathcal{S}_{t}=\bigcup_{s<t}\ \bigcup_{j=1}^{K_{s}}\operatorname{supp}(g^{s,j}). (9)

An algorithm is zero-respecting if, for every admissible instance, its queries and its output after RR rounds satisfy

supp⁡(zt,k)⊆𝒮t,supp⁡((x^,0))⊆𝒮R+1.\operatorname{supp}(z^{t,k})\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{t},\qquad\operatorname{supp}((\hat{x},0))\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{R+1}. (10)

Here (x^,0)∈ℝdx+dy(\hat{x},0)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}+d_{y}} denotes the embedding of the primal output into the joint primal-dual space. The first condition requires every query to use only coordinates revealed by previous oracle gradients, while the second requires every nonzero coordinate of the final output x^\hat{x} to have been revealed by the end of round RR. In particular, let 𝒮1=∅\mathcal{S}_{1}=\emptyset, so first-round queries are at the origin. It covers a lot of algorithms including linear-span algorithms and coordinate-wise updates that preserve zero coordinates.

Complexity measurement.

Our goal is to find the stationary point x^\hat{x} in terms of the expectation, i.e.,

𝔼​‖∇Φ​(x^)‖2≤ϵ2;\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi(\hat{x})\right\rVert^{2}\leq{\epsilon}^{2};

we also give lower bounds for 𝔼​‖∇Φ​(x^)‖≤ϵ\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi(\hat{x})\right\rVert\leq{\epsilon} (refer to Proposition C.2). After RR rounds, the number of oracle calls is N=∑t=1RKtN=\sum_{t=1}^{R}K_{t}. Each returned joint gradient vector counts once, including all minibatch and refresh samples. Let 𝒜zr,N(K)\mathcal{A}_{{\rm zr},N}^{(K)} be the algorithms above using at most NN calls on every run. For either instance class ℐ\mathcal{I}, define

𝒞ϵ,zr(K)(ℐ)=inf{N∈ℕ0:∃A∈𝒜zr,N(K),supI∈ℐ𝔼I‖∇ΦI(x^A)‖2≤ϵ2}.\mathcal{C}_{{\epsilon},{\rm zr}}^{(K)}(\mathcal{I})=\inf\!\left\{N\in\mathbb{N}_{0}:\exists A\in\mathcal{A}_{{\rm zr},N}^{(K)},\ \sup_{I\in\mathcal{I}}\mathbb{E}_{I}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{I}(\hat{x}_{A})\right\rVert^{2}\leq{\epsilon}^{2}\right\}. (11)

The classes range over all finite dimensions; algorithms may know the dimensions and class parameters. Thus a lower bound rules out a uniform guarantee for every algorithm in this class, not just a particular update rule. Our proof bounds rounds first and uses R≤NR\leq N to bound calls, without an extra factor KK. The expected-norm version is defined by replacing the squared norm and ϵ2{\epsilon}^{2} in Equation (11) by the norm and ϵ{\epsilon}.

3.2 Hard Instance Construction

Let H:ℝd→ℝH:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} have an ℓ\ell-Lipschitz gradient, and let gHg_{H} be an unbiased estimator of ∇H\nabla H. For positive h,q,γh,q,\gamma, set

α=q2/h,β=h/q,ν=μ+ℓ​h,\alpha=q^{2}/h,\qquad\beta=h/q,\qquad\nu=\mu+\ell h, (12)

and define the minimax objective

fH​(x,y)=α​H​(β​y)−ν2​‖y−γ​x‖2.f_{H}(x,y)=\alpha H(\beta y)-\frac{\nu}{2}\left\lVert y-\gamma x\right\rVert^{2}. (13)

We evaluate the quadratic gradient exactly and randomize only the estimate of ∇H\nabla H:

Gx=ν​γ​(y−γ​x),Gy=q​gH​(β​y,ξ)−ν⁡(y−γ​x).G_{x}=\nu\gamma(y-\gamma x),\qquad G_{y}=qg_{H}(\beta y;\xi)-\nu(y-\gamma x). (14)

If xi=yi=0x_{i}=y_{i}=0, then [Gx]i=0[G_{x}]_{i}=0 and [Gy]i=q​[gH​(β​y,ξ)]i[G_{y}]_{i}=q[g_{H}(\beta y;\xi)]_{i}. Thus, the quadratic coupling cannot reveal a new coordinate on its own; new coordinates enter the support only through the base oracle gHg_{H}. The following proposition is the main reduction used in proofs.

Proposition 3.1 (Lifted Function).

Suppose HH is twice continuously differentiable and bounded below, with H⁡(0)−infH≤DH(0)-\inf H\leq D and ‖∇H​(0)‖≤g\left\lVert\nabla H(0)\right\rVert\leq g. Then fH​(x,⋅)f_{H}(x,\cdot) is μ\mu-strongly concave and

Lip⁡(∇fH)\displaystyle\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla f_{H}) ≤ν⁡(1+γ2)+ℓ​h,\displaystyle\leq\nu(1+\gamma^{2})+\ell h, (15)
ΦH​(0)−infΦH\displaystyle\Phi_{H}(0)-\inf\Phi_{H} ≤α​D+q2​g22​μ,\displaystyle\leq\alpha D+\frac{q^{2}g^{2}}{2\mu}, (16)
‖∇H​(β​γ​x)‖\displaystyle\left\lVert\nabla H(\beta\gamma x)\right\rVert ≤1+ℓ​h/νγ​q‖∇ΦH(x)‖∀x.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1+\ell h/\nu}{\gamma q}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{H}(x)\right\rVert\qquad\forall x. (17)

If gHg_{H} has variance at most v2v^{2}, the lifted oracle has variance at most q2​v2q^{2}v^{2}. If gHg_{H} has averaged-smoothness constant SS, the lifted constant is at most ν⁡(1+γ2)+h​S\nu(1+\gamma^{2})+hS.

Remark 3.2.

The above result is important and characterizes several important properties of the lifted function fHf_{H}. We want to highlight Equation (17) above, with this lower bound result, we transfer the lower bound study on the primal function ∇ΦH\nabla\Phi_{H} to that of ∇H\nabla H, which is well-studied in nonconvex minimization lower bound literature (Carmon et al., 2020; Arjevani et al., 2023). Moreover, note that

G⁡(x,y,ξ)−∇fH​(x,y)=(0,q⁡[gH​(β​y,ξ)−∇H​(β​y)]).G(x,y;\xi)-\nabla f_{H}(x,y)=\bigl(0,q[g_{H}(\beta y;\xi)-\nabla H(\beta y)]\bigr). (18)

Thus the unbounded quadratic gradient contributes no noise, which allows a uniform variance bound on the whole space.

Choice of HH and gHg_{H}.

Regarding the hard instance function HH and oracle gHg_{H} for lower bound derivations, we take H:ℝT→ℝH:\mathbb{R}^{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} to be the hard instance function introduced by Carmon et al. (2020) (i.e., the function FTF_{T} therein), which satisfies the zero-chain property, and used in the stochastic nonconvex lower bounds of Arjevani et al. (2023). For an integer T≥2T\geq 2, it is defined by

H⁡(u)=−Ψ⁡(1)​Φ0​(u1)+∑i=2T[Ψ⁡(−ui−1)​Φ0​(−ui)−Ψ⁡(ui−1)​Φ0​(ui)],\displaystyle H(u)={}-\Psi(1)\Phi_{0}(u_{1})+\sum_{i=2}^{T}\bigl[\Psi(-u_{i-1})\Phi_{0}(-u_{i})-\Psi(u_{i-1})\Phi_{0}(u_{i})\bigr], (19)

where

Ψ(t)={0,t≤12,exp⁡(1−(2​t−1)−2),t>12,Φ0(t)=e∫−∞te−s2/2ds.\Psi(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t\leq\frac{1}{2},\\ \exp\bigl(1-(2t-1)^{-2}\bigr),&t>\frac{1}{2},\end{cases}\qquad\Phi_{0}(t)=\sqrt{e}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-s^{2}/2}\,ds.

Each summand couples two consecutive coordinates. Starting from the origin, a zero-respecting method using exact gradients can reveal at most one new coordinate per query. Moreover, uT=0u_{T}=0 implies ‖∇H​(u)‖>1\|\nabla H(u)\|>1, so the method must reach the last coordinate before finding a point with a small gradient. The gradient Lipschitz constant is independent of TT, and the initial gap is 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(T).

For the estimator gHg_{H}, we use the stochastic gradient constructions of Arjevani et al. (2023). Additional properties of the resulting stochastic hard instances are collected in Appendix B. In both the BV and AS settings, the lifted constructions preserve the probabilistic zero-chain structure of the underlying hard instance; we describe this property next.

3.3 Probabilistic Zero-Chain Mechanism

For u∈ℝTu\in\mathbb{R}^{T} and a≥0a\geq 0, define

proga⁡(u):=max⁡({i∈{1,…,T}:|ui|>a}∪{0}).\operatorname{prog}_{a}(u):=\max\bigl(\{i\in\{1,\ldots,T\}:|u_{i}|>a\}\cup\{0\}\bigr).

In particular, prog0⁡(u)\operatorname{prog}_{0}(u) is the largest index in supp⁡(u)\operatorname{supp}(u), with value zero when u=0u=0.

Definition 3.3 (First-Order Zero-Chain).

A differentiable function H:ℝT→ℝH:\mathbb{R}^{T}\to\mathbb{R} is a first-order zero-chain if

prog0⁡(∇H​(u))≤prog0⁡(u)+1for every ​u∈ℝT.\operatorname{prog}_{0}(\nabla H(u))\leq\operatorname{prog}_{0}(u)+1\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^{T}.

For a zero-respecting method starting from the origin, an exact-gradient query can therefore reveal at most one new coordinate. The stochastic counterpart controls how often a new coordinate can be revealed. We use the following definition from Arjevani et al. (2023).

Definition 3.4 (Probability-pp Zero-Chain).

Let p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1], and let gH​(u,ξ)g_{H}(u;\xi) be an unbiased gradient estimator of HH. We call gHg_{H} a probability-pp zero-chain (PZC) if

ℙξ(∃u∈ℝT:prog0(gH(u;ξ))=prog1/4(u)+1)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\xi}\!\left(\exists u\in\mathbb{R}^{T}:\operatorname{prog}_{0}(g_{H}(u;\xi))=\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(u)+1\right) ≤p,\displaystyle\leq p, (20)
ℙξ(∃u∈ℝT:prog0(gH(u;ξ))>prog1/4(u)+1)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}_{\xi}\!\left(\exists u\in\mathbb{R}^{T}:\operatorname{prog}_{0}(g_{H}(u;\xi))>\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(u)+1\right) =0.\displaystyle=0.

A single seed is used for all points inside each event. Thus the definition controls an entire same-seed batch, not just each query separately.

Lemma 3.5 (Progress of the Lifted Oracle).

Suppose gHg_{H} is a probability-pp zero-chain in the sense of Definition 3.4, and let GG be the lifted oracle in Equation (14), with dx=dy=Td_{x}=d_{y}=T. For any zero-respecting algorithm following the oracle protocol of Section 3 and returning x^\hat{x} after at most RR rounds,

ℙ⁡(supp⁡(x^)⊆{1,…,T−1})≥1−p​RT.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\operatorname{supp}(\hat{x})\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T-1\}\right)\geq 1-\frac{pR}{T}.

In particular, R≤T/(4​p)R\leq T/(4p) implies ℙ⁡(x^T=0)≥3/4\mathbb{P}(\hat{x}_{T}=0)\geq 3/4.

This adapts the PZC progress argument of Arjevani et al. (2023, Lemma 1) to the quadratic lift. Appendix C detailed the discussion and characterizes the PZC property of the two base oracles, proves Lemma 3.5, and combines it with Equation (17) to obtain the gradient lower bound in Proposition C.2.

4 The Bounded Variance Case Lower Bound

In this section, we derive the lower complexity bound of stochastic NC-SC minimax optimization problems, under the generic bounded variance setting.

Theorem 4.1 (Bounded Variance).

There are universal constants c,c0>0c,c_{0}>0 such that, for L,μ,Δ>0L,\mu,\Delta>0, σ≥0\sigma\geq 0, κ=L/μ≥8\kappa=L/\mu\geq 8, and 0<ϵ2≤c0​L​Δ0<{\epsilon}^{2}\leq c_{0}L\Delta,

𝒞ϵ,zr(1)​(ℐBV​(L,μ,Δ,σ))≥c​L​Δϵ2​max⁡{1,κ​σ2ϵ2}.\mathcal{C}_{{\epsilon},{\rm zr}}^{(1)}\bigl(\mathcal{I}_{\rm BV}(L,\mu,\Delta,\sigma)\bigr)\geq c\frac{L\Delta}{{\epsilon}^{2}}\max\left\{1,\frac{\kappa\sigma^{2}}{{\epsilon}^{2}}\right\}. (21)

The same order holds for the expected-norm target. The hard instances have actual smoothness-to-strong-concavity ratio within universal constant factors of κ\kappa.

Proof Sketch.

We use the hard instance function and oracle as discussed in Section 3.2, which are motivated by Carmon et al. (2020); Arjevani et al. (2023). Its gradient stays bounded away from zero until its last coordinate is reached. The oracle reveals the next coordinate with probability at most pp, with variance 𝒪⁡(p−1)\mathcal{O}(p^{-1}) independent of TT. In Equation (12), we choose

γ2≍κ,q2≍ϵ2/κ,h≍μ,p≍min⁡{1,ϵ2/(κ​σ2)},\gamma^{2}\asymp\kappa,\qquad q^{2}\asymp{\epsilon}^{2}/\kappa,\qquad h\asymp\mu,\qquad p\asymp\min\{1,{\epsilon}^{2}/(\kappa\sigma^{2})\}, (22)

where p=1p=1 when σ=0\sigma=0. Proposition 3.1 guarantees that the stationarity transfer fixes γ​q\gamma q at a constant multiple of ϵ{\epsilon}. A zero-respecting algorithm needs order T/pT/p rounds to reveal the chain. The dependence on κ\kappa comes from the smaller reveal probability. Appendices B to D present the detailed oracle definition, support argument, and all parameter checks.

Comparison with Existing Results.

The previous lower bound for the BV setting is Ω⁡(κ1/3​ϵ−4)\Omega(\kappa^{1/3}{\epsilon}^{-4}) (Li et al., 2021). Our Theorem 4.1 strengthens the dependence on the condition number from κ1/3\kappa^{1/3} to κ\kappa, while allowing both the primal and dual variables to remain unconstrained. On the upper-bound side, SAPD+ and SPDE achieve a leading stochastic complexity of 𝒪⁡(κ​ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}(\kappa{\epsilon}^{-4}) for Moreau-envelope stationarity (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026). In Section 5.2, we extend our lower bound to the same stationarity criterion, while Section 5.3 discusses the remaining differences in assumptions.

5 The Averaged-Smooth Lower Bound

Building on the BV analysis, we now impose the additional averaged-smoothness assumption on the stochastic oracle and derive a sharper lower bound.

Theorem 5.1 (Averaged Smoothness).

There are universal constants c,c0,c1>0c,c_{0},c_{1}>0 such that the following holds for every fixed finite K≥1K\geq 1. Let L¯,μ,Δ>0\overline{L},\mu,\Delta>0, σ≥0\sigma\geq 0, κ=L¯/μ≥8\kappa=\overline{L}/\mu\geq 8, and suppose

0<ϵ2≤c0​L¯​Δ,ϵ​σ≤c1​L¯​Δ​κ.0<{\epsilon}^{2}\leq c_{0}\overline{L}\Delta,\qquad{\epsilon}\sigma\leq c_{1}\overline{L}\Delta\sqrt{\kappa}. (23)

Then

𝒞ϵ,zr(K)​(ℐAS​(L¯,μ,Δ,σ))≥c​L¯​Δϵ2​max⁡{1,min⁡{κ​σ2ϵ2,κ3/2​σϵ}}.\mathcal{C}_{{\epsilon},{\rm zr}}^{(K)}\bigl(\mathcal{I}_{\rm AS}(\overline{L},\mu,\Delta,\sigma)\bigr)\geq c\frac{\overline{L}\Delta}{{\epsilon}^{2}}\max\left\{1,\min\left\{\frac{\kappa\sigma^{2}}{{\epsilon}^{2}},\frac{\kappa^{3/2}\sigma}{{\epsilon}}\right\}\right\}. (24)

The same order holds for the expected-norm target.

5.1 Proof Sketch

The stochastic oracle used in the BV analysis does not, in general, satisfy the averaged-smoothness requirement. We therefore adopt the smooth-gating construction of Arjevani et al. (2023), which preserves variance of order 𝒪⁡(p−1)\mathcal{O}(p^{-1}) while achieving an averaged-smoothness constant of order 𝒪(p−1/2)\mathcal{O}(p^{-1/2}). As a consequence, Proposition 3.1 imposes the additional constraint h≲min⁡{μ,L¯​p}h\lesssim\min\{\mu,\overline{L}\sqrt{p}\}. With the same choices γ2≍κ\gamma^{2}\asymp\kappa and q2≍ϵ2/κq^{2}\asymp{\epsilon}^{2}/\kappa as in the BV case, the resulting complexity scales as

Tp≍Δ​hq2​p≍L¯​Δϵ2min{p−1,κp−1/2}.\frac{T}{p}\asymp\frac{\Delta h}{q^{2}p}\asymp\frac{\overline{L}\Delta}{{\epsilon}^{2}}\min\left\{p^{-1},\kappa p^{-1/2}\right\}. (25)

Choosing p≍min⁡{1,ϵ2/(κ​σ2)}p\asymp\min\{1,{\epsilon}^{2}/(\kappa\sigma^{2})\} then yields Equation (24). The conditions in Equation (23) ensure that the chain length is admissible and that the initial primal gap remains within Δ\Delta. Full calibration details are given in Appendix E.

Returning to Equation (24), the lower bound can be expressed across three regimes:

L¯​Δ​ϵ−2×{1,σϵ−1≤κ−1/2,κ​σ2​ϵ−2,κ−1/2<σϵ−1<κ,κ3/2​σ​ϵ−1,σ​ϵ−1≥κ.\overline{L}\Delta{\epsilon}^{-2}\times\begin{cases}1,&\sigma{\epsilon}^{-1}\leq\kappa^{-1/2},\\ \kappa\sigma^{2}{\epsilon}^{-2},&\kappa^{-1/2}<\sigma{\epsilon}^{-1}<\sqrt{\kappa},\\ \kappa^{3/2}\sigma{\epsilon}^{-1},&\sigma{\epsilon}^{-1}\geq\sqrt{\kappa}.\end{cases} (26)

In particular, in the high-accuracy regime, where ϵ{\epsilon} is sufficiently small, the lower bound reduces to Ω⁡(L¯​Δ​κ3/2​σ​ϵ−3)\Omega(\overline{L}\Delta\kappa^{3/2}\sigma{\epsilon}^{-3}). Moreover, when L=L¯L=\overline{L}, the AS lower bound is always no larger than the corresponding BV lower bound.

5.2 Lower Bounds for Moreau Envelope Stationarity

Theorems 4.1 and 5.1 measure stationarity using the primal gradient. But recent NC-SC literature of SAPD+ and SPDE (Zhang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026) used Moreau envelope stationarity as the measurement. Our primal stationarity lower bound results in Theorem 5.1 does not provide a lower bound for this criterion, so a separate transfer is needed. Set M=LM=L in the BV setting and M=L¯M=\overline{L} in the AS setting, and define

Pf​(x):=Φ1/(2​M)​(x)=minu∈ℝdx⁡{Φ⁡(u)+M​‖u−x‖2}.P_{f}(x):=\Phi_{1/(2M)}(x)=\min_{u\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}}\{\Phi(u)+M\left\lVert u-x\right\rVert^{2}\}. (27)

Lemma A.1 ensures that PfP_{f} is well-defined and continuously differentiable.

On the hard instances used in our proofs, the two stationarity measures are equivalent up to universal constants. Specifically, Lemma F.2 shows that

123128​‖∇PfH​(x)‖≤‖∇ΦH​(x)‖≤133128​‖∇PfH​(x)‖for every ​x.\frac{123}{128}\left\lVert\nabla P_{f_{H}}(x)\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{H}(x)\right\rVert\leq\frac{133}{128}\left\lVert\nabla P_{f_{H}}(x)\right\rVert\qquad\text{for every }x. (28)

Thus here a small Moreau-envelope gradient would also imply a small primal gradient, with a constant factor independent of κ\kappa. Combining this comparison with the primal-gradient lower bounds in Proposition C.2, we have the following result.

Corollary 5.2 (Moreau Envelope Lower Bounds).

The lower bounds in Theorems 4.1 and 5.1 also hold, up to universal constant factors, when the required output satisfies either

𝔼​‖∇Pf​(x^)‖2≤ϵ2or𝔼⁡‖∇Pf​(x^)‖≤ϵ.\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla P_{f}(\hat{x})\right\rVert^{2}\leq{\epsilon}^{2}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla P_{f}(\hat{x})\right\rVert\leq{\epsilon}.

Here the parameters, oracle protocols, and algorithm class are unchanged.

Appendix F proves the gradient comparison and the corollary. Both gradients are evaluated at the algorithm’s output, so no additional oracle call or proximal computation is needed. The resulting bounds preserve the dependence on κ\kappa and ϵ{\epsilon} and can be compared directly with upper bounds stated for Moreau-envelope stationarity.

5.3 Comparison with Existing Upper Bounds

For primal stationarity, SREDA established 𝒪⁡(κ3​ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{3}{\epsilon}^{-3}) SFO complexity under averaged smoothness (Luo et al., 2020), while it further assumes a compact dual domain and sample-wise concavity. Its expected-norm criterion is also covered by our lower bounds (refer to Proposition C.2). For Moreau envelope stationarity, SAPD+ (Zhang et al., 2024, the revised version) gives

𝒪⁡(L​𝒢0ϵ2​max⁡{κ,σ/ϵ}​(1+κ​σ/ϵ))\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{L\mathcal{G}_{0}}{{\epsilon}^{2}}\max\{\kappa,\sqrt{\sigma/{\epsilon}}\}(1+\kappa\sigma/{\epsilon})\right) (29)

for its variance-reduced variant (Zhang et al., 2024), where 𝒢0\mathcal{G}_{0} is the initial primal-dual gap. Consequently, its bound is not uniformly 𝒪⁡(κ2​ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\kappa^{2}{\epsilon}^{-3}) as accuracy ϵ→0{\epsilon}\rightarrow 0.

More recently, Zhang et al. (2026) proposed VR-SPDE and obtained 𝒪⁡(L¯​κ3/2​σ​ϵ−3)\mathcal{O}(\overline{L}\kappa^{3/2}\sigma{\epsilon}^{-3}) for the AS case. By Corollary 5.2, we can find that the result of Zhang et al. (2026) tightly matches our lower bound in the high-accuracy regime. Also as shown in Table 1 and Figure 1, in the low-accuracy regime, the 𝒪⁡(κ​ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}(\kappa{\epsilon}^{-4}) upper bound by SAPD+ (Zhang et al., 2024) also tightly matches our lower bound, so our lower bound reveals the optimal SFO complexity in terms of κ\kappa and ϵ{\epsilon} for the AS case.

6 Conclusion and Future Work

We establish stochastic first-order lower bounds for fully unconstrained NC-SC minimax optimization over zero-respecting algorithms. For sufficiently small ϵ{\epsilon}, we prove lower bounds of Ω⁡(L​Δ​κ​σ2​ϵ−4)\Omega(L\Delta\kappa\sigma^{2}{\epsilon}^{-4}) under bounded variance and Ω⁡(L¯​Δ​κ3/2​σ​ϵ−3)\Omega(\overline{L}\Delta\kappa^{3/2}\sigma{\epsilon}^{-3}) under averaged smoothness. Both results follow from a unified construction that couples a nonconvex zero-chain with a deterministic quadratic lifting, and both extend to Moreau envelope stationarity without worsening the dependence on κ\kappa. These lower bounds match recent stochastic upper bounds in terms of their dependence on κ\kappa and ϵ{\epsilon}.

Several questions remain open. First, it would be useful to extend the lower bounds beyond zero-respecting algorithms to more general, possibly randomized, first-order methods. Another direction is to better align the domain and initialization assumptions in upper and lower bounds. Finally, our zero-chain hard instances require a dimension that grows with the target accuracy; whether comparable lower bounds hold in fixed or low dimensions, in the spirit of Chewi et al. (2023), remains open.

Appendix A Preliminaries and proof of the quadratic lift

We collect the standard value-function properties, prove Proposition 3.1, and verify the actual condition numbers of the constructed instances.

A.1 Standard value-function properties

The following lemma supplies the facts used in Section 3 and in the Moreau-envelope argument of Appendix F. The sensitivity and differentiability statements are standard; see Sinha et al. (2017, Lemma 1) and Lin et al. (2020b, Lemma 4.3). The envelope formula is given in Lin et al. (2020a, Lemma 17).

Lemma A.1 (Primal function and Moreau envelope).

Let M,μ>0M,\mu>0, and let f:ℝdx×ℝdy→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}}\to\mathbb{R} be continuously differentiable, with an MM-Lipschitz gradient, and suppose f⁡(x,⋅)f(x,\cdot) is μ\mu-strongly concave for every xx. Then y∗​(x):=arg⁡maxy⁡f⁡(x,y)y^{*}(x):=\arg\max_{y}f(x,y) exists uniquely, the value function Φ⁡(x):=maxy⁡f⁡(x,y)\Phi(x):=\max_{y}f(x,y) is continuously differentiable, and

Lip⁡(y∗)≤Mμ,∇Φ​(x)=∇xf​(x,y∗​(x)),Lip⁡(∇Φ)≤M⁡(1+Mμ).\operatorname{Lip}(y^{*})\leq\frac{M}{\mu},\qquad\nabla\Phi(x)=\nabla_{x}f(x,y^{*}(x)),\qquad\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla\Phi)\leq M\left(1+\frac{M}{\mu}\right). (30)

Moreover, Φ\Phi is MM-weakly convex. If infΦ>−∞\inf\Phi>-\infty, then

ux:=arg⁡minu​{Φ⁡(u)+M​‖u−x‖2}u_{x}:=\arg\min_{u}\{\Phi(u)+M\left\lVert u-x\right\rVert^{2}\}

exists uniquely, and the Moreau envelope Pf:=Φ1/(2​M)P_{f}:=\Phi_{1/(2M)} satisfies

∇Pf​(x)=2​M​(x−ux)=∇Φ​(ux).\nabla P_{f}(x)=2M(x-u_{x})=\nabla\Phi(u_{x}). (31)
Proof.

Strong concavity gives

f⁡(x,y)≤f⁡(x,0)+⟨∇yf​(x,0),y⟩−μ2​‖y‖2⟶−∞(‖y‖→∞),f(x,y)\leq f(x,0)+\left\langle\nabla_{y}f(x,0),y\right\rangle-\frac{\mu}{2}\left\lVert y\right\rVert^{2}\longrightarrow-\infty\quad(\left\lVert y\right\rVert\to\infty),

so the inner maximum is attained uniquely on the full space. The joint smoothness assumption bounds each blockwise Lipschitz constant by MM. Applying Sinha et al. (2017, Lemma 1) with these constants gives Equation (30). For each fixed yy, the function f⁡(⋅,y)+M​‖⋅‖2/2f(\cdot,y)+M\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert^{2}/2 is convex; its pointwise supremum is Φ+M​‖⋅‖2/2\Phi+M\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert^{2}/2, proving weak convexity. When infΦ>−∞\inf\Phi>-\infty, the proximal objective is coercive and MM-strongly convex, so uxu_{x} exists uniquely. Lin et al. (2020a, Lemma 17) gives the first equality in Equation (31); the second is the first-order optimality condition at uxu_{x}. ∎

A.2 Proof of Proposition 3.1

The smoothness, gap, and oracle estimates are used in Appendices D and E; the stationarity transfer is used in Proposition C.2.

Proof of Proposition 3.1.

Strong concavity, smoothness, and gap. Since α​β=q\alpha\beta=q and α​β2=h\alpha\beta^{2}=h,

∇xfH=νγ(y−γx),∇yfH=q∇H(βy)−ν(y−γx).\nabla_{x}f_{H}=\nu\gamma(y-\gamma x),\qquad\nabla_{y}f_{H}=q\nabla H(\beta y)-\nu(y-\gamma x). (32)

The bound ‖∇2H‖≤ℓ\left\lVert\nabla^{2}H\right\rVert\leq\ell gives ∇y​y2fH=h​∇2H​(β​y)−ν​I⪯−μ​I\nabla_{yy}^{2}f_{H}=h\nabla^{2}H(\beta y)-\nu I\preceq-\mu I. The Hessian of the quadratic coupling is

−ν​(γ2​I−γ​I−γ​II),-\nu\begin{pmatrix}\gamma^{2}I&-\gamma I\\ -\gamma I&I\end{pmatrix},

whose operator norm is ν⁡(1+γ2)\nu(1+\gamma^{2}). The remaining Hessian has norm at most ℓ​h\ell h, proving Equation (15). Lemma A.1 now gives a unique inner maximizer and the primal-gradient formula.

At the origin, smoothness of HH yields

fH​(0,y)≤α​H​(0)+q⁡⟨∇H​(0),y⟩−μ2​‖y‖2,ΦH​(0)≤α​H​(0)+q2​g22​μ.f_{H}(0,y)\leq\alpha H(0)+q\left\langle\nabla H(0),y\right\rangle-\frac{\mu}{2}\left\lVert y\right\rVert^{2},\qquad\Phi_{H}(0)\leq\alpha H(0)+\frac{q^{2}g^{2}}{2\mu}.

For any xx, the feasible choice y=γ​xy=\gamma x gives

ΦH​(x)≥α​H​(β​γ​x)≥α​infH>−∞.\Phi_{H}(x)\geq\alpha H(\beta\gamma x)\geq\alpha\inf H>-\infty. (33)

Subtracting this lower bound from the bound at the origin proves Equation (16).

Explicit stationarity transfer. Set z∗=β​y∗​(x)z^{*}=\beta y^{*}(x) and w=β​γ​xw=\beta\gamma x. The inner first-order condition and the primal-gradient formula give

z∗−w=hν∇H(z∗),∇ΦH(x)=γq∇H(z∗).z^{*}-w=\frac{h}{\nu}\nabla H(z^{*}),\qquad\nabla\Phi_{H}(x)=\gamma q\nabla H(z^{*}). (34)

Consequently,

‖∇H​(w)‖≤‖∇H​(z∗)‖+ℓ⁡‖w−z∗‖≤(1+ℓ​hν)​‖∇H​(z∗)‖,\left\lVert\nabla H(w)\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert\nabla H(z^{*})\right\rVert+\ell\left\lVert w-z^{*}\right\rVert\leq\left(1+\frac{\ell h}{\nu}\right)\left\lVert\nabla H(z^{*})\right\rVert,

which proves Equation (17). For the scaled function Hsc​(u):=α​H​(β​u)H_{\rm sc}(u):=\alpha H(\beta u), this also gives

‖∇Hsc​(γ​x)‖≤1+ℓ​h/νγ​‖∇ΦH​(x)‖.\left\lVert\nabla H_{\rm sc}(\gamma x)\right\rVert\leq\frac{1+\ell h/\nu}{\gamma}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{H}(x)\right\rVert.

Stochastic oracle. The error identity Equation (18) and unbiasedness of gHg_{H} give unbiasedness of GG and the variance bound q2​v2q^{2}v^{2}. If gHg_{H} has root mean-squared Lipschitz constant at most SS, then Minkowski’s inequality gives

(𝔼​‖G⁡(z,ξ)−G⁡(z′,ξ)‖2)1/2\displaystyle\bigl(\mathbb{E}\left\lVert G(z;\xi)-G(z^{\prime};\xi)\right\rVert^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} ≤ν⁡(1+γ2)​‖z−z′‖+q​S​‖β⁡(y−y′)‖\displaystyle\leq\nu(1+\gamma^{2})\left\lVert z-z^{\prime}\right\rVert+qS\left\lVert\beta(y-y^{\prime})\right\rVert
≤[ν⁡(1+γ2)+h​S]​‖z−z′‖,\displaystyle\leq[\nu(1+\gamma^{2})+hS]\left\lVert z-z^{\prime}\right\rVert,

which concludes the proof. ∎

A.3 Actual condition numbers

The next lemma is used in the class-membership checks in Appendices D and E. It establishes the actual-condition-number statements in Theorems 4.1 and 5.1.

Lemma A.2 (Condition numbers of the lift).

Consider the construction of Proposition 3.1. Suppose γ2=M/(4​μ)\gamma^{2}=M/(4\mu), ℓ​h≤μ/4\ell h\leq\mu/4, and Lip⁡(∇fH)≤M\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla f_{H})\leq M. Let μact\mu_{\rm act} be the largest uniform inner strong-concavity modulus, and let Lact:=Lip⁡(∇fH)L_{\rm act}:=\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla f_{H}). Then, for κ=M/μ\kappa=M/\mu,

κ6≤Lactμact≤κ.\frac{\kappa}{6}\leq\frac{L_{\rm act}}{\mu_{\rm act}}\leq\kappa. (35)

If the lifted oracle also has root mean-squared Lipschitz constant at most MM, its smallest such constant L¯act\overline{L}_{\rm act} satisfies the same bounds: κ/6≤L¯act/μact≤κ\kappa/6\leq\overline{L}_{\rm act}/\mu_{\rm act}\leq\kappa.

Proof.

The inner Hessian bounds imply

μ≤μact≤ν+ℓ​h≤3​μ2.\mu\leq\mu_{\rm act}\leq\nu+\ell h\leq\frac{3\mu}{2}. (36)

Holding yy fixed and changing xx gives, for every seed,

‖∇fH​(x,y)−∇fH​(x′,y)‖\displaystyle\left\lVert\nabla f_{H}(x,y)-\nabla f_{H}(x^{\prime},y)\right\rVert =‖G⁡(x,y,ξ)−G⁡(x′,y,ξ)‖\displaystyle=\left\lVert G(x,y;\xi)-G(x^{\prime},y;\xi)\right\rVert (37)
=ν​γ​1+γ2​‖x−x′‖.\displaystyle=\nu\gamma\sqrt{1+\gamma^{2}}\left\lVert x-x^{\prime}\right\rVert.

Since ν​γ​1+γ2≥ν​γ2≥M/4\nu\gamma\sqrt{1+\gamma^{2}}\geq\nu\gamma^{2}\geq M/4, we obtain Lact≥M/4L_{\rm act}\geq M/4 and, when finite, L¯act≥M/4\overline{L}_{\rm act}\geq M/4. Combining these estimates with Equation (36) and the assumed upper bounds proves the claims. ∎

Appendix B The base chain and its stochastic oracles

B.1 The nonconvex chain

Recall that we define H=FTH=F_{T} in Equation (19) where FTF_{T} is adapted from Carmon et al. (2020): for T≥2T\geq 2, define

Ψ(t)={0,t≤1/2,exp⁡(1−(2​t−1)−2),t>1/2,Φ0(t)=e∫−∞te−s2/2ds,\Psi(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t\leq 1/2,\\ \exp\bigl(1-(2t-1)^{-2}\bigr),&t>1/2,\end{cases}\qquad\Phi_{0}(t)=\sqrt{e}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-s^{2}/2}\,ds,

and

FT​(u)=−Ψ⁡(1)​Φ0​(u1)+∑i=2T[Ψ⁡(−ui−1)​Φ0​(−ui)−Ψ⁡(ui−1)​Φ0​(ui)].F_{T}(u)=-\Psi(1)\Phi_{0}(u_{1})+\sum_{i=2}^{T}\bigl[\Psi(-u_{i-1})\Phi_{0}(-u_{i})-\Psi(u_{i-1})\Phi_{0}(u_{i})\bigr]. (38)

For a≥0a\geq 0, write proga⁡(u)=max⁡({i:|ui|>a}∪{0})\operatorname{prog}_{a}(u)=\max(\{i:|u_{i}|>a\}\cup\{0\}). Both Ψ\Psi and Φ0\Phi_{0} are bounded, so FTF_{T} is bounded below. We use the following published properties.

Lemma B.1 (Properties of FTF_{T} (Arjevani et al., 2023)).

The function FTF_{T} is twice continuously differentiable and satisfies

FT​(0)−infFT\displaystyle F_{T}(0)-\inf F_{T} ≤12​T,\displaystyle\leq 12T, (39)
Lip⁡(∇FT)\displaystyle\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla F_{T}) ≤152,‖∇FT​(u)‖∞≤23,\displaystyle\leq 152,\quad\left\lVert\nabla F_{T}(u)\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq 23, (40)
prog0⁡(∇FT​(u))\displaystyle\operatorname{prog}_{0}(\nabla F_{T}(u)) ≤prog1/2⁡(u)+1,\displaystyle\leq\operatorname{prog}_{1/2}(u)+1, (41)
prog1⁡(u)<T\displaystyle\operatorname{prog}_{1}(u)<T ⟹‖∇FT​(u)‖>1.\displaystyle\ \Longrightarrow\ \left\lVert\nabla F_{T}(u)\right\rVert>1. (42)

In particular, ‖∇FT​(0)‖≤23\left\lVert\nabla F_{T}(0)\right\rVert\leq 23.

Based on the chain of Carmon et al. (2020). The bound at zero follows from Equation (41) and the coordinate bound. We take this lemma as the external analytic input; the lift, oracle estimates, progress argument, and parameter choices are proved here.

B.2 A bounded-variance oracle

Let Z∼Bernoulli⁡(p)Z\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) with 0<p≤10<p\leq 1 and define

[gTBV(u;Z)]i=∇iFT(u)[1+𝟏{i>prog1/4(u)}(Z/p−1)].[g_{T}^{\rm BV}(u;Z)]_{i}=\nabla_{i}F_{T}(u)\left[1+\mathbf{1}\{i>\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(u)\}(Z/p-1)\right]. (43)

Since 𝔼⁡(Z/p−1)=0\mathbb{E}(Z/p-1)=0, the estimator is unbiased. Moreover, prog1/2⁡(u)≤prog1/4⁡(u)\operatorname{prog}_{1/2}(u)\leq\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(u). By Equation (41), its error can have at most one nonzero coordinate, namely prog1/4⁡(u)+1\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(u)+1 when this index is at most TT. Hence

𝔼​‖gTBV​(u,Z)−∇FT​(u)‖2≤232​1−pp.\mathbb{E}\left\lVert g_{T}^{\rm BV}(u;Z)-\nabla F_{T}(u)\right\rVert^{2}\leq 23^{2}\frac{1-p}{p}. (44)

The new frontier coordinate can be nonzero only when Z=1Z=1. This is the bounded-variance construction in Arjevani et al. (2023, equation (17)); the argument above verifies the properties needed for the lift.

B.3 An averaged-smooth oracle

We specify a single smooth gate before choosing any problem parameters. Let

Λ⁡(t)={exp⁡(−1100​(t−1/4)​(1/2−t)),1/4<t<1/2,0,otherwise,Γ⁡(t)=∫1/4tΛ⁡(s)​𝑑s∫1/41/2Λ⁡(s)​𝑑s.\Lambda(t)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{100(t-1/4)(1/2-t)}\right),&1/4<t<1/2,\\[2.0pt] 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\Gamma(t)=\frac{\int_{1/4}^{t}\Lambda(s)\,ds}{\int_{1/4}^{1/2}\Lambda(s)\,ds}.

Then 0≤Γ≤10\leq\Gamma\leq 1, Γ=0\Gamma=0 on (−∞,1/4](-\infty,1/4], Γ=1\Gamma=1 on [1/2,∞)[1/2,\infty), and mΓ:=supt|Γ′​(t)|<∞m_{\Gamma}:=\sup_{t}|\Gamma^{\prime}(t)|<\infty is a universal constant. This is the smooth gate used by Arjevani et al. (2023). For the tail u≥i=(ui,…,uT)u_{\geq i}=(u_{i},\ldots,u_{T}), set

Θi​(u)=Γ⁡(1−‖Γ⁡(|u≥i|)‖),[gTAS​(u,Z)]i=∇iFT​(u)​[1+Θi​(u)​(Z/p−1)],\Theta_{i}(u)=\Gamma\bigl(1-\left\lVert\Gamma(|u_{\geq i}|)\right\rVert\bigr),\qquad[g_{T}^{\rm AS}(u;Z)]_{i}=\nabla_{i}F_{T}(u)[1+\Theta_{i}(u)(Z/p-1)], (45)

where the inner Γ\Gamma is applied coordinatewise. The flat regions of Γ\Gamma give

𝟏{i>prog1/4(u)}≤Θi(u)≤𝟏{i>prog1/2(u)}.\mathbf{1}\{i>\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(u)\}\leq\Theta_{i}(u)\leq\mathbf{1}\{i>\operatorname{prog}_{1/2}(u)\}. (46)

Indeed, a tail bounded by 1/41/4 gives inner norm zero and outer value one; a tail containing an entry larger than 1/21/2 gives inner norm at least one and outer value zero.

For g=23g=23 and any ℓ≥152\ell\geq 152, the oracle Equation (45) is unbiased, and for all u,vu,v,

We prove Lemma 3.5 and the stationarity bound used in Appendices D-F. Write [m]={1,…,m}[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\} for integers m≥0m\geq 0, with [0]=∅[0]=\varnothing.

Lemma C.1 (PZC property of the base oracles (Arjevani et al., 2023, Lemmas 3-4)).

For every T≥2T\geq 2 and p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1], the oracles gTBVg_{T}^{\rm BV} in Equation (43) and gTASg_{T}^{\rm AS} in Equation (45) are probability-pp zero-chains in the sense of Definition 3.4. For either oracle, with Z∼Bernoulli⁡(p)Z\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p),

prog0(gT(u;Z))≤prog1/4(u)+𝟏{Z=1}for every u∈ℝT and Z∈{0,1}.\operatorname{prog}_{0}(g_{T}(u;Z))\leq\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(u)+\mathbf{1}\{Z=1\}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^{T}\text{ and }Z\in\{0,1\}.

Let ℰ\mathcal{E} be the first event in Definition 3.4. Outside a null set of seeds, that definition gives, simultaneously for all uu,

prog0(gH(u;ξ))≤prog1/4(u)+𝟏{ξ∈ℰ}≤prog0(u)+𝟏{ξ∈ℰ}.\operatorname{prog}_{0}(g_{H}(u;\xi))\leq\operatorname{prog}_{1/4}(u)+\mathbf{1}\{\xi\in\mathcal{E}\}\leq\operatorname{prog}_{0}(u)+\mathbf{1}\{\xi\in\mathcal{E}\}.

Set J0=0J_{0}=0 and Jt=∑s=1t𝟏{ξs∈ℰ}J_{t}=\sum_{s=1}^{t}\mathbf{1}\{\xi_{s}\in\mathcal{E}\}. Write Gbt,k=Gb​(zt,k,ξt)G_{b}^{t,k}=G_{b}(z^{t,k};\xi_{t}) for b∈{x,y}b\in\{x,y\}. Induction gives, almost surely, for every actual query and response,

supp⁡(xt,k)∪supp⁡(yt,k)\displaystyle\operatorname{supp}(x^{t,k})\cup\operatorname{supp}(y^{t,k}) ⊆[Jt−1],\displaystyle\subseteq[J_{t-1}], (49)
supp⁡(Gxt,k)∪supp⁡(Gyt,k)\displaystyle\operatorname{supp}(G_{x}^{t,k})\cup\operatorname{supp}(G_{y}^{t,k}) ⊆[Jt].\displaystyle\subseteq[J_{t}].

The first queries are at the origin; thereafter, zero-respecting gives the first inclusion from the earlier response supports. The coupling terms in Equation (14) are supported within [Jt−1][J_{t-1}]. This proves the second inclusion for every kk with the same seed ξt\xi_{t}.

If the algorithm stops after τ≤R\tau\leq R rounds, the output restriction gives supp⁡(x^)⊆[Jτ]⊆[JR]\operatorname{supp}(\hat{x})\subseteq[J_{\tau}]\subseteq[J_{R}]; unused seeds through round RR may be sampled independently for this argument. Since ℙ⁡(ξt∈ℰ)≤p\mathbb{P}(\xi_{t}\in\mathcal{E})\leq p, we have 𝔼​JR≤p​R\mathbb{E}J_{R}\leq pR. Markov’s inequality now yields

ℙ⁡(supp⁡(x^)⊈[T−1])≤ℙ⁡(JR≥T)≤p​RT.∎\mathbb{P}\!\left(\operatorname{supp}(\hat{x})\not\subseteq[T-1]\right)\leq\mathbb{P}(J_{R}\geq T)\leq\frac{pR}{T}.\qed
Proposition C.2 (Stationarity lower bound).

Let H=FTH=F_{T} with T≥2T\geq 2, let ϵ>0{\epsilon}>0, and use either base oracle from Lemma C.1 in the lift Equation (14). Suppose γ​q=8​ϵ\gamma q=8{\epsilon} and ℓ​h/ν≤1/5\ell h/\nu\leq 1/5. For every admissible zero-respecting algorithm using at most R≤T/(4​p)R\leq T/(4p) rounds,

ℙ⁡(‖∇ΦH​(x^)‖>203​ϵ)≥34.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{H}(\hat{x})\right\rVert>\frac{20}{3}{\epsilon}\right)\geq\frac{3}{4}. (50)

Consequently,

𝔼⁡‖∇ΦH​(x^)‖≥5​ϵ,𝔼​‖∇ΦH​(x^)‖2≥1003​ϵ2.\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{H}(\hat{x})\right\rVert\geq 5{\epsilon},\qquad\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{H}(\hat{x})\right\rVert^{2}\geq\frac{100}{3}{\epsilon}^{2}. (51)

Lemmas C.1 and 3.5 give ℙ⁡(x^T=0)≥3/4\mathbb{P}(\hat{x}_{T}=0)\geq 3/4. On this event, (β​γ​x^)T=0(\beta\gamma\hat{x})_{T}=0, so Lemma B.1 gives ‖∇FT​(β​γ​x^)‖>1\left\lVert\nabla F_{T}(\beta\gamma\hat{x})\right\rVert>1. The stationarity transfer Equation (17) implies

Appendix F Proof of the Moreau-envelope lower bounds

We prove Corollary 5.2 in three steps: bound the smoothness of the primal function on the hard family, compare its gradient with the Moreau-envelope gradient, and apply Proposition C.2. Throughout, M=LM=L for BV and M=L¯M=\overline{L} for AS.

Proposition F.1 (Primal smoothness).

For the lift in Proposition 3.1,

Lip⁡(∇ΦH)≤ν​γ2​ℓ​hμ.\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla\Phi_{H})\leq\frac{\nu\gamma^{2}\ell h}{\mu}. (63)

Under either parameter choice in Appendices D-E, this upper bound is at most 5​M/645M/64.

Proof.

The inner optimality condition is

q∇H(βy∗(x))=ν(y∗(x)−γx).q\nabla H(\beta y^{*}(x))=\nu\bigl(y^{*}(x)-\gamma x\bigr).

For two points x,x′x,x^{\prime}, write y=y∗​(x)y=y^{*}(x) and y′=y∗​(x′)y^{\prime}=y^{*}(x^{\prime}). Subtracting their optimality conditions gives

ν⁡(y−y′)=ν​γ​(x−x′)+q⁡(∇H​(β​y)−∇H​(β​y′)).\nu(y-y^{\prime})=\nu\gamma(x-x^{\prime})+q\bigl(\nabla H(\beta y)-\nabla H(\beta y^{\prime})\bigr).

Since HH has an ℓ\ell-Lipschitz gradient and q​β=hq\beta=h,

ν⁡‖y−y′‖≤ν​γ​‖x−x′‖+ℓ​h​‖y−y′‖.\nu\left\lVert y-y^{\prime}\right\rVert\leq\nu\gamma\left\lVert x-x^{\prime}\right\rVert+\ell h\left\lVert y-y^{\prime}\right\rVert.

‖y∗​(x)−y∗​(x′)‖≤ν​γμ​‖x−x′‖.\left\lVert y^{*}(x)-y^{*}(x^{\prime})\right\rVert\leq\frac{\nu\gamma}{\mu}\left\lVert x-x^{\prime}\right\rVert. (64)

∇ΦH(x)=νγ(y∗(x)−γx)=γq∇H(βy∗(x)).\nabla\Phi_{H}(x)=\nu\gamma\bigl(y^{*}(x)-\gamma x\bigr)=\gamma q\nabla H(\beta y^{*}(x)).

Consequently,

≤ν​γ2​ℓ​hμ​‖x−x′‖.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\nu\gamma^{2}\ell h}{\mu}\left\lVert x-x^{\prime}\right\rVert.

Lemma F.2 (Equivalence of stationarity measures on the hard family).

Under either calibration in Appendices D and E, let PfH=(ΦH)1/(2​M)P_{f_{H}}=(\Phi_{H})_{1/(2M)}. Then, for every xx,

123128​‖∇PfH​(x)‖≤‖∇ΦH​(x)‖≤133128​‖∇PfH​(x)‖.\frac{123}{128}\|\nabla P_{f_{H}}(x)\|\leq\|\nabla\Phi_{H}(x)\|\leq\frac{133}{128}\|\nabla P_{f_{H}}(x)\|.

Proof of Corollary 5.2.

Fix either the BV or AS setting and choose exactly the same hard instance and parameters as in its lower-bound proof in Appendix D or E. An algorithm using at most N≤T/(4​p)N\leq T/(4p) oracle calls also uses at most T/(4​p)T/(4p) rounds. Proposition C.2 therefore gives

𝔼⁡‖∇ΦH​(x^)‖≥5​ϵ,𝔼​‖∇ΦH​(x^)‖2≥1003​ϵ2.\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{H}(\hat{x})\right\rVert\geq 5{\epsilon},\qquad\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\nabla\Phi_{H}(\hat{x})\right\rVert^{2}\geq\frac{100}{3}{\epsilon}^{2}.

≥1003​(128133)2​ϵ2>ϵ2.\displaystyle\geq\frac{100}{3}\left(\frac{128}{133}\right)^{2}{\epsilon}^{2}>{\epsilon}^{2}.

Thus neither Moreau-envelope criterion can be met within the same oracle budget.
